figures.caption: Discrete point-group identification across equivariant GNNs. a, Point-group identification accuracy and rank-template match rate across GNN architectures and training states. citing_sentences: In Fig. 2a, point-group identification accuracy reaches or closely approaches the $30/32$ template-based limit at $l=0,\ldots,6$, with consistently high rank-template match rates across models and training states.

In Fig. 2b, PF and all randomly initialized GNNs attain the same identification accuracy at a shared relative rank tolerance, showing that a common numerical threshold suffices across models (Table C.5).

2c), combining node and edge representations reaches the identification limit at $l=0,\ldots,6$, and varying the number or width of the radial bases leaves identification accuracy unchanged (Table C.6).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: SymFP tracks symmetry breaking and distinguishes deformation modes. All panels use PF at $l=0,\ldots,6$. a, Symmetry breaking immediately activates new singular values, whose number matches the change in the rank template induced by the deformation. Structural illustrations show the three deformations, and curves show the corresponding singular-value trajectories at selected degrees. b, Along the subgroup chain, spectral tail energies relative to the target point groups rise in sequence and follow the theoretically predicted subgroup monotonicity. Vertical dashed lines mark the symmetry-breaking transitions. c, Four deformation modes of the same $\mathrm{C}_{6}$ structure with equal RMSD. d, Self-match RMSD between a deformed structure and its $60^{\circ}$-rotated copy, computed using corresponding points and illustrated for the in-plane stretch. e, Self-match RMSD (top) and degree-resolved relative tail energy (bottom) as functions of deformation amplitude for the four modes in c. The self-match RMSD curves for the four modes largely overlap in pairs, whereas spectral onset degrees further distinguish their angular differences. Relative tail energies below $10^{-9}$ are displayed in a separate numerical-floor strip.
figures.headline: Symmetry breaking activates singular values that match rank-template changes, and tail energy rises in subgroup order.
citing_sentences: 3a), the number of activated singular values agrees exactly with the rank template predictions as symmetry is reduced.
3b), where the spectral tail energy for each target group rises sharply upon symmetry breaking before levelling off, while the relative magnitudes across groups verify subgroup monotonicity.
3c), we apply four deformations with equal RMSD to the same structure: axial staircase, in-plane stretch, in-plane radial, and axial pucker.

figures.caption: Symmetry and energy-extremum retrieval along biaryl torsions. Throughout, SymFP uses PF representations with uniform pooling over natural-parity degrees $l=0,2,4,6$. a, Biphenyl torsion schematic and evaluated cohort: 86 molecules, 24 conformations each at $15^{\circ}$ increments, with deposited coordinates and quantum-mechanical (QM) energies. b, Biphenyl conformations ranked by descending even-degree negative-log leakage score (pLS) for the $\mathrm{D_{2h}}$ target. Coral downward and blue-grey upward triangles mark minima and maxima in the QM energy profile; grey dots mark other conformations. Shading marks the first eight conformations, and the arrow indicates increasing the selection budget. The four maxima rank $1$–$4$ and the four minima rank $7$–$10$, so the first ten of the $24$ conformations recover all eight sampled energy extrema. c, Energy-extremum recall against the selected fraction of conformations over 94 molecule–target pairs from 86 molecules. Extrema are defined relative to both periodic neighbours in the deposited energy profile. The inset enlarges the 10–25% selection range. Mean areas under the recall–budget curve (AUC) are $0.794$, $0.747$ and $0.787$ for SymFP, CSoM and Engel score, respectively, compared with a random-ranking expectation of $0.5$. At a $25\%$ selection budget, the corresponding recall values are $68.8\%$, $66.9\%$ and $66.3\%$. d, Mean AUC for minima and maxima separately. For SymFP, CSoM and Engel score, respectively, AUCs are $0.720$, $0.647$ and $0.735$ for minima and $0.867$, $0.847$ and $0.839$ for maxima. e, Per-molecule AUC differences (SymFP minus baseline). CSoM is sign-reversed, and each score profile is independently scaled to [0,1], so that higher values indicate greater target agreement.

abstract: Symmetry governs the organization of physical structures, while symmetry breaking reveals their transformations. In geometric deep learning, symmetry imposes rank constraints on equivariant representations, limiting the expressive capacity of equivariant graph neural networks (GNNs). Here we show that these constraints can instead be exploited: the singular-value spectra of equivariant representations provide a unified fingerprint of structural symmetry. We introduce spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP), which enable discrete point-group identification through rank-template matching and continuous symmetry analysis by quantifying spectral energy beyond target rank constraints. SymFP is orientation invariant and architecture agnostic, enabling a parameter-free GNN implementation. Its spectra can be reused across multiple target groups, and the resulting leakage scores satisfy subgroup monotonicity. Across synthetic structures, molecules, coordination complexes and large biological assemblies, SymFP accurately identifies point groups, tracks controlled symmetry breaking and reveals local and degree-resolved symmetry changes that can be obscured by global geometric measures. These results establish the spectral structure of equivariant representations as a general framework for characterizing symmetry across physical systems.

sections.body: The section frames structural symmetry as two tasks: discrete point-group identification and continuous symmetry analysis. It argues that equivariant representations are a natural starting point, because their rank constraints depend on the point group. The authors build spectral symmetry fingerprints (SymFP) from singular-value spectra across degrees, and define leakage scores (LS) and their pooled negative-log form (pLS). They compare these with continuous symmetry measures (CSMs), the continuous symmetry operation measure (CSoM), and Engel score. The text states that SymFP needs no symmetric reference structures or orientation searches, and that it satisfies subgroup monotonicity. Evaluations cover synthetic structures, aromatic molecules, DOTA complexes and large biological assemblies.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: The paper treats structural symmetry as two tasks, point-group identification and continuous analysis, and proposes spectral fingerprints from equivariant representations for both.

sections.body: SymFP collects the ordered singular values of each degree-wise equivariant representation across degrees 0 to L. Under exact symmetry, the rank of each representation is bounded by the fixed-subspace dimension, which defines a rank template for each point group. Degrees 0 to 6 give 30 distinct templates across the 32 crystallographic point groups, and degrees 0 to 9 distinguish all 32. Leakage score (LS) is the normalized spectral energy beyond the target dimensions, and pLS is its negative-log transform, with a maximum value of 10. Subgroup monotonicity follows from larger fixed subspaces giving equal or lower leakage. The authors note that representations span the full fixed subspaces in most tested cases.
sections.heading: Results
sections.headline: Singular-value spectra of equivariant representations define a fingerprint that matches point groups through rank templates and scores symmetry leakage.

sections.body: The discussion states that SymFP turns symmetry constraints on equivariant representations into structural information, giving one framework for point-group identification and continuous analysis. It says the constraints come from the algebraic structure of the representations rather than any particular message-passing implementation, so the approach applies across equivariant GNN architectures. The parameter-free implementation builds representations directly from geometry. The authors suggest the perspective may extend to space groups, chirality and helical symmetries, and could help study phase transitions, defect evolution and amorphization. This section reports no new experiments.
sections.heading: Discussion
sections.headline: The constraints come from representation algebra, so the framework may extend beyond point groups to space groups and chirality.

sections.body: The methods define a geometric graph as compatible with a finite point group when each group element permutes nodes while preserving coordinates, attributes and adjacency. The stabilizer of a graph gives its exact point group when finite. Representations use natural-parity real Wigner-D matrices for O(3). The section reviews continuous symmetry measures based on distance to the nearest compatible realization, and the continuous symmetry operation measure, which averages operation-wise deviations. For biaryl torsion scans it uses 94 molecule–target pairs from 86 molecules. Lanthanide analyses use seven water-free complexes. Water rotation uses pLS pooled over degrees 0 to 6.
sections.heading: Methods
sections.headline: Methods define graph compatibility, stabilizers and O(3) representations, and the datasets used for each analysis.

sections.body: This section lists where the data come from. Synthetic point clouds cover the 32-group benchmark, controlled symmetry-breaking families and matched-amplitude displacement fields, and are generated deterministically. The biaryl torsion study uses relaxed scans from OpenFF Rowley Biaryl v1.0, obtained through QCArchive. The lanthanide DOTA study uses a water-free Ln(DOTA) series deposited as CCDC 2281329 and 2281615 to 2281620, plus two approximate analogues and a capping-water trajectory. The assemblies are Protein Data Bank entries, such as 8FCL and 6Y5G. The accompanying repository provides point clouds, dataset splits, selections and source data.
sections.heading: Data availability
sections.headline: Synthetic point clouds, Protein Data Bank entries and OpenFF torsion scans are the data sources behind the reported analyses.

sections.body: This section gives the code location and the tools it depends on. The SymFP implementation, training code and evaluation scripts are released at a GitHub repository. Point-group analysis and space-group expansion use pymatgen. Implementation details for the equivariant GNNs are provided in the repository. HEGNN uses a multi-channel extension developed in this work, which is included there. CSoM is evaluated with the software released by its authors. Engel score is the authors' own implementation of the published construction.
sections.heading: Code availability
sections.headline: The SymFP implementation, training code and evaluation scripts are released in a GitHub repository.

It does not describe any other relationships. Readers seeking further detail on the authors should consult the full manuscript.

sections.body: The appendix collects Extended Data Figures 1 to 5 and supplementary tables. Extended Data Fig. 1 shows spectral responses of the parameter-free model and four learnable equivariant GNNs at random initialization. The other figures cover p97 neighbourhood and window checks, haemagglutinin regional responses, GluK2 spatial layers and E18 icosahedral agreement. Table D.9 lists onset degrees for four deformation modes, and Table D.10 gives haemagglutinin self-match residuals. The E18 degree-six pLS falls from 6.56 in the intact capsid to 1.65, 1.15 and 0.85 when one, two or three pentamers are missing.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists Extended Data figures and tables on GNN spectra, p97, haemagglutinin, GluK2 and E18 capsids.
